curve-lab · G3 catalogue

Every candidate, as a G3 quintic interpolation

This page shows the interpolation, not the ideal curve. Each admitted curve is a chain of quintic Bézier spans, five to fourteen spans per branch, with every join measured G3: position, direction, bend, and the smooth acceleration of the bend. The ideal curve is the faint dashed line underneath. The named curves are read from their exact homogeneous control polygons; the hearts, presets, primals and recovered LAC/Stage II spines are read from a local cubic fit of their sampled polylines. A branch that cannot be interpolated G3 — a cusp, a point at infinity, a singular handle solve, or a deviation over 5% of its own size — is rejected and named in the table, not quietly dropped. The interpolation runs from end to end; only when an endpoint is singular (a cusp or a point at infinity) is the first or last span trimmed, and the panel says so.

How admission works. The knots are placed at equal arc length on the curve. At each knot the tangent, curvature and curvature-rate are read from the exact homogeneous control polygon, or from a local cubic fit for the sampled hearts, presets, primals and spines. The quintic span matches them at both ends, and the two handle lengths are chosen to minimise the deviation from the ideal. The table's max deviation is a geometric distance, not a parameter error. A curve is admitted only when the deviation is under 5% of its own size; the rejected reasons state the measured share. The G3 gate is computed from the Bézier derivatives, not from the drawn polyline. Two exemptions are declared: the closure seam — the point where a closed shape starts and ends — and a cusp, which is split into smooth arcs. Neither is a body join; a body join at an acute angle, a curvature jump or a curvature-rate jump still fails.

Handover to Inkscape and the glyph pipeline

The unit is the finished curve, not the span. A curve is G3-complete when every interior join — including the closure seam of a closed form and every mirror seam — matches position, tangent, curvature and curvature-rate, and every break is declared by the source (a cusp, a node, or a singular endpoint), not created by the fit. A smooth handover is a G3-complete curve that is one path with no declared feature, whose deviation is under 5% of its size, and whose spans keep a speed above 10% of their chord. That is the list to give Inkscape or a glyph editor without a smoothness caveat.

The interior-speed gate. A join-only test can pass two spans that each graze a near-cusp in their interior: the ends match, but the span's speed falls toward zero and dκ/ds spikes by many orders of magnitude. A span is admitted only when its speed never falls below 10% of its chord. This is what makes the acceleration graphs readable and the smooth badge honest; a row that fails it is rejected with the measured speed floor, not quietly drawn flat.

Why a quintic is the carrier. Fixing both endpoints, a G3 join asks for six conditions (tangent direction, curvature and curvature-rate at each end) against eight unknowns in a quintic span; the two left over are the handle lengths used to follow the source. A quartic has no freedom left; a cubic is over-determined. So a quintic span is the least span that can meet G3 at both ends. The number of spans is a property of the assembly — mirror seams, cusps, nodes and fidelity knots — not of the degree.

Mirror seams are benign, and testable. If a curve crosses a mirror axis orthogonally, reflection preserves curvature (κ is a scalar invariant), so κ is continuous; κ is even about the seam, so dκ/ds is odd and must vanish there. A true mirror of a smooth half is therefore G3 at the seam automatically, and dκ/ds = 0 is the test that the mirror is true. An oblique crossing fails even G1; a mirror tangent (the two arcs meeting with opposite tangents) is a cusp, not a smooth seam, and is declared as one.

The closure seam is not an exemption. Where a closed curve starts is an artifact of the parameterisation, so the seam must pass like any other join. If it fails, either re-knot the span decomposition or place the seam at a declared node or cusp. The nodal loops in this catalogue (bow, strophoid, bernoulli, nodal, abs-Gerono) declare a node at the seam; they are complete with that feature, not smooth.

Native degree. A quintic span is a pure degree elevation of a cubic when its fifth divided difference vanishes: P0 − 5P1 + 10P2 − 10P3 + 5P4 − P5 = 0. Then the fifth-degree freedom did no work, and the row is badged cubic-native: a simple curve collapsing to a cubic is a selector signal, not an accident. A nonzero fifth difference with a zero fourth difference is quartic-native; everything else genuinely uses the quintic. The badge is derived from the control polygon, never asserted.

Rejected, with the reason

A cusp has no tangent direction, so G3 is undefined there; a point at infinity has no finite position. These are not failures of the interpolation — they are curves outside the G3 domain. A few hearts are rejected because the quintic G3 spans cannot follow their sharp features within 5% of the curve size; the reason gives the measured share. The squircle is still sampled only and needs the same polyline treatment. The next pass adds it and tightens the high-error cases with more spans.

Back to the G3 showcase · theory on the G3 notes page · terminals on the extend-and-cut page.

Cusp curves · allowed with a declared cusp

A cusp is a declared feature, not a G3 join. The curve is split into smooth arcs between cusps; G3 applies to the arcs, not to the cusp itself. The astroid is admitted as four such arcs (max deviation 0.0074). The other -oids and the cardioid were already admitted.

Cusped hearts already admitted: heart · cardioid, heart · |x|^(2/3) upper, heart · |x|^(2/3) lower, heart · Valentine, heart · Wolfram, heart · Kuriscak upper, heart · Kuriscak lower, heart · Wu–Nick lower …. See the Heart forms group.

Still failing · deviation

These are not cusp failures. They are source curves whose best quintic interpolation still misses by more than 5% of the curve size; they stay visible instead of being quietly dropped. The squircle is the clearest case.
